summary.text: At \(n=67\), the distinct integers \(147\) and \(2055\) both have the required residue sum: \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\) and \(1+3+9\cdot7=67\), respectively. Thus there are at least two occurrences, contradicting the asserted value \(a(67)=1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 m\rfloor}\bigl(m\bmod 2^k\bigr)
\]
be the sequence A049802. Thus A383327 is the multiplicity function
\[
a(n)=\#\{m:F(m)=n\}.
\]
Equivalently, in the finite counting formulation used here for positive \(n\), one counts those \(m<2^{n+1}\) for which \(F(m)=n\); the bound is sufficient for all such occurrences. For the disproof below, it is enough in either formulation to exhibit two distinct integers in that range having value \(67\) under \(F\).

We claim that both
\[
m_1=147 \qquad\text{and}\qquad m_2=2055
\]
satisfy \(F(m_i)=67\).

First consider \(147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\), so the relevant moduli are \(2,4,8,16,32,64,128\). Write \(147=128+19\). Because \(128\) is divisible by every \(2^k\) for \(1\le k\le7\), the residue of \(147\) modulo \(2^k\) is the same as the residue of \(19\) modulo \(2^k\). Consequently,
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
147\bmod 2^k&1&3&3&3&19&19&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, \(19\equiv1\pmod2\), \(19\equiv3\pmod4\), \(19\equiv3\pmod8\), \(19\equiv3\pmod{16}\), and \(19<2^k\) for \(k=5,6,7\). Therefore
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19
      =1+9+57
      =67.
\]

Now consider \(2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Write \(2055=2048+7\). The number \(2048=2^{11}\) is divisible by \(2^k\) for every \(1\le k\le11\), so the residue of \(2055\) modulo \(2^k\) equals that of \(7\). For \(k=1\) this residue is \(1\), for \(k=2\) it is \(3\), and for every \(k=3,4,\ldots,11\) it is \(7\), since \(7<2^k\). There are nine indices from \(3\) through \(11\), inclusive. Hence
\[
F(2055)=1+3+\underbrace{7+\cdots+7}_{9\text{ terms}}
       =1+3+9\cdot7
       =67.
\]

The integers \(147\) and \(2055\) are distinct. They also both lie in the finite search range used to define \(a(67)\): plainly
\[
147<2055<2^{68}=2^{67+1}.
\]
Thus the set
\[
\{m<2^{68}:F(m)=67\}
\]
contains at least the two distinct elements \(147\) and \(2055\). It follows that
\[
a(67)\ge2,
\]
and in particular \(a(67)\ne1\).

Finally, \(67\) is one of the integers in the conjectured set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts that \(a(n)=1\) for every member of this set, so it asserts in particular that \(a(67)=1\). This contradicts \(a(67)\ge2\). Therefore the conjecture is false.
